name: Founder story in one moment
aka: origin story; why I started; founding moment
shape: The founder opens inside one scene from their past: a place, a date, a feeling. They tell that single moment like a short story, then link it in one or two sentences to why the company exists today. The name, the title and the résumé come last, or stay out.

name: Founder journey montage (day 1 to day 1,000)
aka: journey montage; thousand days in; milestone montage
shape: A fast montage of clips filmed since the first day of the company, in order, with a voice-over that counts the time in months and days. The voice names two or three hard moments as the clips pass. The last shot shows where the company stands today.

name: Mission launch: the problem nobody fixed, so we built it
aka: launch video; mission video; so we built it
shape: The founder names a big problem that everyone has accepted for years. They say they got tired of waiting for someone else to fix it, and reveal what the team built. The product is shown working, and the video ends with where to get it.

name: Credential hook, then three tips
aka: here is how; authority hook list; three tips
shape: The first sentence promises how to get a result. The second gives the one credential that lets the speaker say it. Then come three numbered tips, one sentence each, delivered fast to camera.

name: Contrarian hot take with proof
aka: hot take; you are doing it wrong; contrarian opener
shape: The speaker opens by telling the viewer they are doing something wrong, or that they should skip what everyone does. The next line is personal proof: what the speaker did or tried. Then the reasoning in three short beats, to camera.

name: The tirade: unscripted yapping on one opinion
aka: yapping; la tirade; car rant; raw monologue
shape: The founder holds the phone on the front camera, in a car or while walking, and talks without a script about one opinion they could defend for an hour. Few cuts, high energy, real pauses. The energy is the hook, and the opinion is the payoff.

name: Myth vs data
aka: debunk; myth busting; the data says otherwise
shape: The speaker states a belief their market keeps repeating and says plainly that it is wrong. Then they show the number or the mechanism that breaks it, often on a greenscreen. The video ends with what to do instead.

name: Company expert grades the myths (A to F)
aka: myth grades; expert report card; our scientist rates
shape: The company's expert (chief scientist, CTO, head of research) reads popular claims of the category one by one. Each claim gets a letter grade and one sentence of evidence. The video is posted from the brand account, often as a recurring series.

name: Two experts rate the hacks (and disagree)
aka: hacks rated 0 to 10; two experts rate; cofounders rate
shape: Two experts sit side by side facing the camera. A popular hack from their field appears, and both say their score from 0 to 10 at the same moment. When the scores clash, each defends theirs in a sentence, and the disagreements carry the fun.

name: The dated bet: mark my words
aka: mark my words; the bet; bold prediction
shape: The founder opens with a bold prediction about their category, with a date attached ("X won't exist within 20 years"). They name the experience behind the bet, then list the signals that support it. The video closes on what would prove them wrong.

name: One number, explained
aka: one stat; the craziest statistic; number of the day
shape: One statistic fills the screen in the first second. The speaker explains what it really means, why most people misread it, and what it changes for the viewer. One number per video, with the source visible.

name: Industry insider alert: what nobody tells you
aka: insider alert; what nobody tells you; industry secret
shape: An insider reveals a practice of their own industry that works against customers. They explain how it works with one concrete example. The video ends with what viewers can do to protect themselves.

name: Storytime during a routine task (GRWM style)
aka: get ready with me; GRWM storytime; pack orders with me
shape: The speaker does a mundane task on camera (getting ready, making coffee, packing orders) while telling a personal story with a cliffhanger. The task gives the eyes something to follow, and the story gives the ears a reason to stay. The task and the story end together.

name: Read the post that changed my mind
aka: I think about this weekly; let me read this to you; the thread that changed me
shape: The speaker puts a post, thread or email on screen with a greenscreen. They say how long ago they read it and how often they still think about it. Then they read the key lines aloud and explain how it changed the way they work.

name: Your flaw is your job (reframe list)
aka: flaw to job; reframe list; you talk too much start a podcast
shape: A fast list of flaws people are told they have, each one answered at once by a job or a move that turns it into an asset ("You talk too much. Start a podcast."). The speaker delivers it to camera with a steady rhythm. Each pair takes a few seconds.

name: Breaking down my own mistake
aka: my mistake broken down; public post-mortem; yes that was me
shape: The founder admits a public mistake in the first line ("Yes, that's me who..."). They replay it on screen, then break it down step by step: the context, the decision, and what they would do now. The post-mortem is published openly.

name: Open product decision: option A or option B
aka: behind the build; option A or option B; why we are waiting
shape: The founder explains a real product or launch decision as a choice between two options. They lay out the trade-off of each, in plain words. The video ends with the option the team picked, or with the decision still open and a question to viewers.

name: Build log: does it work yet?
aka: build log; building in public; test of the day
shape: One episode of a build in progress. The founder says what they are making, where they are, and runs the test of the day on camera. The episode ends on whether it worked, and failures are shown as openly as wins.

name: Countdown to save the company (day X)
aka: save my company; day X of 30; help us survive
shape: A real deadline the business must beat (a debt, a stock to sell, a closure date) becomes a numbered series. Each episode gives the count, the progress since last time, and one thing viewers can do to help. The series ends when the deadline passes, whatever the outcome.

name: Bad news: we are closing (or this is the last batch)
aka: we have bad news; closing announcement; last batch
shape: The founder opens with "we have bad news" and announces an end: the company closes, a product is discontinued, or the last stock is going. They say what they tried before deciding. The video ends with what happens now for customers and followers.

name: Money talk: what it really cost
aka: what it really cost; the real price; budget breakdown
shape: The founder opens on a real amount ("330,000 euros is what we paid"). Then comes the breakdown, the part that blew up the budget, and what the viewer should plan for if they try the same thing. Filmed to camera, often where the money was spent.

name: How I make money, explained at my stand
aka: here's how I make money; business model explained; I'm 25 and
shape: The founder opens with their age and "here's how I make money", then explains the business model in plain words. They stand where the business happens (a stall, a workshop, a desk) with the product in hand. The viewer leaves understanding exactly who pays and for what.

name: The objection, answered
aka: objection video; isn't that a bad idea; the doubt answered
shape: The founder says out loud the objection buyers raise most, or the doubt people have about the business itself. Then they answer it with one fact and one example. The video ends on what the viewer should take from the answer.

name: Founder responds to a review
aka: founder reacts to a review; brand answers the reviewer; review response
shape: The founder plays a creator's review of their own product, pausing after each criticism. They answer point by point: they agree where the reviewer is right, explain the trade-off behind each choice, and say what is coming next. The video ends on the one point the founder is proudest of.

name: Comment reply with a full video
aka: reply with video; comment answer; FAQ video
shape: One comment appears on screen through the platform's reply-with-video sticker. The speaker reads it, then answers it fully in one video. When a thread has hundreds of comments, the speaker picks the most recurring question and says so in the first line.

name: Backlash follow-up: you said I was wrong
aka: response to backlash; part 2 after the comments; you said I was wrong
shape: After a video triggers pushback, the creator comes back with the critical comments on screen. They say plainly what they got right and what they got wrong. Then they settle the question with evidence: a source, a demo or a term the critics used.

name: Comment reply acted out (the boss says answer every comment)
aka: my boss says I have to respond to all the comments; acted comment reply; comment skit
shape: The video opens on the frame line "my boss says I have to respond to all the comments". A real comment appears on screen, and the team acts it out literally as a short scene in the shop or the office. Each episode takes one comment, so the frame line repeats and the series becomes recognizable.

name: Insider: I designed it, here is what users did
aka: designer's commentary; what users did with my feature; we built it for X
shape: The person who built a feature or a product says who they are and what they intended. Then they show, with real footage or screen recordings, what users actually did with it, things the designer never saw coming. The video ends with what the team learned or changed because of it.

name: Odd-setting cold open
aka: you might be wondering why I'm here; weird location opener; setting as metaphor
shape: The video opens with the speaker in an unexpected place or situation, and the first line names it ("You might be wondering why I'm sitting in a kayak"). The speaker explains how they got there, and the place turns into the metaphor for the point they want to make. The ending ties the setting back to the lesson.

name: Name the behavior nobody named
aka: there is a name for this; behavior naming; coined term explainer
shape: The speaker describes a behavior almost everyone has, in enough detail that the viewer recognizes themselves. Then they give it a name, explain why it happens, and say what to do about it. The name is the part people repeat, comment and share.

name: The third option
aka: false choice reveal; there is a third way; A or B or C
shape: The speaker describes the choice the viewer thinks they face: option A or option B, each with its pain. Then they reveal a third option most people have never heard of, explain how it works, and say who it fits. The video ends on the one condition that makes the third option the right pick.

name: Ironic how-to: the fake easy way, then the real one
aka: it's easy; you just...; ironic tutorial; what 99% of people do
shape: The speaker opens with the "easy" advice everyone repeats, delivered deadpan with heavy irony: wake up at 6, plan everything, track every number. Then they show what most people really do, which is far messier. They finish with a simple method that works for real people.

name: Verdict-first monologue
aka: answer first script; verdict then escalation; talking-head escalation
shape: A talking-head script that gives the verdict in the very first line. Next, the speaker says out loud the sensible first reading a viewer would have, then tops it with one plain fact about a third of the way in. From there the script escalates, pushing the key word of the hook to its most extreme meaning by the end.

name: New gadget explained in 60 seconds
aka: new tech explained; this just dropped; gadget news
shape: A new product or device is on screen in the first second. The speaker says what it does, how it works, its price or availability, and one reason it matters. The video ends on what this release means for the field.

name: Industry news explained in 24 hours
aka: news explainer; what just happened; daily news recap
shape: One piece of news from the field, posted within a day of it breaking. The speaker stands in front of the headline or the source document and says what happened, why it happened, and what it changes for the viewer. The video ends on the one thing to watch next.

name: Famous company story in 60 seconds
aka: company story explainer; business story short; how X really started
shape: The speaker tells the surprising arc of a well-known company as a story: the failure, the pivot, the outcome. Photos, headlines and footage play behind or between the lines. The first sentence compresses the whole arc into one twist, and the last sentence lands a punchline or a lesson.

name: Who is this person? (photo explainer)
aka: so this is...; person explainer; who is this guy
shape: A photo of a person fills the background, and the speaker opens with "So this is [name]". They say who the person is, the one thing they changed, and why it still matters today, in simple words. More photos and documents follow as the story moves forward.

name: Everyday analogy for a hard concept
aka: explain it like a burger; analogy explainer; the everyday version
shape: The speaker starts with an everyday situation everyone has lived, such as a burger whose price jumps between the menu and the bill. They walk through it in a few seconds, then map it step by step onto a hard concept from their field. The video ends when the viewer can explain the concept with the everyday words.

name: Why does this exist? (history of an everyday thing)
aka: why is it like this; the origin of; history explainer
shape: The speaker asks why an everyday thing is the way it is, often with a surprising claim about it. Then they tell the short history that explains it, with images from each period. The video ends back in the present, with the thing seen differently.

name: Scale shock: you have no idea how big X is
aka: size comparison; how big is it really; scale explainer
shape: A voice claims that people underestimate the size of something. Then a series of visual comparisons makes the scale felt, each one bigger than the last, using maps, overlays or familiar objects. The final comparison is the most striking and closes the video.

name: Pop culture characters as your industry's archetypes
aka: each character is a type of; film cast as coworkers; archetype mapping
shape: The speaker takes the cast of a famous film or series and maps each character to a type of person in the viewer's world: employees, customers, investors. A still of each character appears behind the speaker while they describe the matching type in one or two lines. The video ends on the character the viewer is most likely to be, or to work with.

name: Fiction vs reality (the film got it wrong)
aka: movies vs real life; what it really looks like; the real story behind
shape: The speaker shows how a game, a film or a cliché depicts something. Then they show what it really looks like, or how it really happened, side by side or one after the other. Each pair repeats the same rhythm: the fiction, then the reality, then one line on the gap.

name: Read the label
aka: ingredient reading; let's see what's inside; terms and conditions read-through
shape: The expert holds a product or shows its label, terms or spec sheet, and reads it line by line. Each line gets a short deadpan comment, often mocking the fear people attach to harmless items. The expert separates real issues from fear-mongering and ends with a calm verdict.

name: Viral hack fact-check: does it work?
aka: does it actually work; hack debunk; expert checks a trend
shape: The speaker shows a viral hack or claim, often by playing or screenshotting it. They ask "does it actually work?", check the evidence or test it, and give a clear verdict. The video ends with the safe or realistic version the viewer can use.

name: This or that, answered
aka: A or B; which one is better; the debate settled
shape: The speaker asks a question with two answers people argue about, often on location where the question lives. They give a clear verdict in the first seconds. Then they explain the reason most people miss, which is the real value of the video.

name: Yes or no, no debate
aka: yes or no without debating; yes or no challenge; rapid-fire yes or no
shape: Someone fires short questions about one topic, and the expert answers each one with a single word: yes or no. The questions come fast, one per second or two, and some answers go against what most people believe. The video ends on the last answer, with zero explanation.

name: Country by country rapid list
aka: if you're selling to X; one rule per buyer; persona rapid list
shape: The speaker goes through a series of groups (countries, personas, buyer types) and gives one rule for each in one sentence. The pattern repeats: "If you're selling to X, do this. To Y, never do that." There is no intro and no wrap-up, only the list delivered fast.

name: From level 1 to pro: the progression
aka: levels of a practice; from your first day to the top; beginner to pro ranking
shape: The video walks through the levels of a practice in order, from the very first day to the top. Each level gets a name and a short picture of what that person looks like: their gear, their habits, their mistakes. Viewers place themselves on the ladder as it climbs.

name: Level-up quiz
aka: if you've seen one of these go to the next level; what level are you; level challenge
shape: The screen shows three items and one rule: "If you know one of these, go to the next level." Each round shows three harder items. The viewer keeps going until they drop out, then comments the level they reached.

name: Everything I do for X in 60 seconds
aka: my whole routine in 60 seconds; every tool I use for X; full stack in one minute
shape: The speaker announces the promise ("I'm going to walk you through everything I do for X in 60 seconds") and then runs a fast montage of every step, tool or ritual. Each item gets one shot and one line of voice. The video ends when the list is complete, close to the minute.

name: Bro vs pro
aka: amateur vs expert; beginner vs pro split screen; what amateurs do vs what pros do
shape: The same person plays two characters side by side: the amateur ("bro") and the expert ("pro"). The bro says one careless line, the pro answers with what they do instead and the reason behind it. Five or six exchanges follow, and the last one lands the biggest gap.

name: Escalating personas
aka: same character at rising stakes; levels of investment skit; I put in more each time
shape: One person plays several versions of the same character, each at a higher stake. Every new version opens with the same sentence and a bigger number, then shows what changes in their day at that level. The last version reaches a level where the habits become absurd or surprising.

name: Logic puzzle with a twist
aka: silly problem serious method; solving everyday problems with algorithms; overkill solution
shape: The speaker states a silly everyday problem as if it were a serious puzzle. Then they solve it with a real method from their field, drawn on a board or on screen, step by step. The twist is the contrast: a trivial goal, a rigorous method, and a solution that actually works.

name: Expert redesign of a real case
aka: expert makeover; let me show you what I'd change; real case redesign
shape: The video opens on a real person's problem in one sentence. The expert shows the current state (a plan, a screen, a room), diagnoses what goes wrong, then builds the redesign step by step. It ends on the before and after side by side.

name: Live teardown of a real document
aka: the teardown; pitch deck breakdown; let me walk you through it
shape: The expert opens a real document from their field on screen (a pitch deck, an email, a landing page, a viral video) and walks through it part by part. At each slide or section, they point at what makes it work and say why. The expert stays visible in a corner or in front of the document with a greenscreen.

name: Numbered daily series (day 16 of 30)
aka: day X of Y; one tip a day; episode series
shape: Every video opens with the same sentence: the series name, the counter and who you are ("Day 16 of pitch deck tips from me, a venture capitalist"). Then one tip or one example, delivered in under two minutes. The series name and the counter stay identical from episode to episode.

name: Detail breakdown: watch this one thing
aka: watch this detail; why is this so good; one detail breakdown
shape: The expert plays a scene, a song or a product on screen and asks the viewer to watch one small detail ("Watch this curtain"). They replay the moment, point at the detail each time it appears and explain how it holds the whole thing together. Once seen, the detail is impossible to miss.

name: The story behind the object
aka: origin story of an object; how this came to exist; the history of a thing
shape: The video shows one object up close, then tells the unlikely story of how it came to exist or came to be used. The story has a setup (who needed it and why), a turn (the strange request or accident) and a payoff (where the object ended up). The object stays on screen or comes back at the end.

name: Cold-open history story
aka: in medias res story; start in the middle; true story cold open
shape: The video drops the viewer in the middle of the most dramatic moment of a true story, with zero context. Then it rewinds to explain who these people were and how they got there. It closes on the lesson the story teaches.

name: Draw while you tell the story
aka: drawn story; sketch explainer; draw my story
shape: The camera looks down on hands drawing on paper or a tablet. A voice tells a story or explains a mechanism, and the drawing builds at the same pace as the story. By the end, the finished drawing sums up the whole story in one image.

name: The famous study, retold
aka: famous experiment story; psychology study explained; what this experiment shows
shape: The speaker tells a famous experiment as a story: who ran it, what the setup was, what people expected and what really happened. The surprising result lands in the middle. The last part applies the lesson to the viewer's work or life.

name: Map explainer
aka: explained on a map; geography explainer; map zoom story
shape: A map fills the screen and a voice explains a crisis, a market or a culture through it. The map zooms in on a place, draws a flow (a river, a trade route, a supply chain) or colors regions as the story moves. The speaker can stand in front of the map with a greenscreen or stay off screen.

name: Animated explainer (inside the machine)
aka: 3D explainer; what happens inside; animated how it works
shape: A 2D or 3D animation travels inside something people cannot see: a cell, a machine, a model, a data pipeline. A simple voice-over narrates each step as the camera moves through it. The video ends when the process completes and the camera pulls back out.

name: Imagine-this voice-over
aka: imagine explaining; imagine it's the year; vision voice-over
shape: A calm voice asks the viewer to imagine a situation ("Imagine it's the year 2256"), and the footage shows something ordinary from a new angle. As the voice describes the scene, everyday things start to feel extraordinary. The video ends on one sentence that turns the feeling back on the viewer's own life.

name: Expert reacts to a fail
aka: fail breakdown; pro reacts; expert stitch
shape: A fail clip from your field plays on screen. The expert pauses it at the key moment, points at what went wrong, and says what a pro would do instead. The clip resumes so the viewer sees the consequence.

name: Reaction with a running counter
aka: counting reaction; tally reaction
shape: A source video plays on one half of the screen and the reactor on the other. A big counter on screen tracks one absurd thing in the video (items ordered, steps taken, tools opened), and it ticks up every time it happens. The reactor's disbelief grows with the number.

name: Respectful debunk of a big creator
aka: claim check; fact check reaction; point by point debunk
shape: A short excerpt of a bigger creator or coach making a claim plays first. The expert then checks it point by point, with a source, a chart or a demo on screen for each point. The tone stays calm and the video ends on what is actually true.

name: Celebrity clip, expert lens
aka: expert analyzes a celebrity; famous clip breakdown
shape: A clip of a famous person plays behind the expert on a greenscreen. The expert stops it at two or three moments and points out what only their trade can see: a word choice, a gesture, a decision. The viewer leaves seeing the famous moment differently.

name: Podcast clip: one strong idea, captioned
aka: podcast short; clip of the episode; captioned clip
shape: The strongest minute of a long conversation, cut so the first words are the claim itself. Word-by-word captions run across the screen, and the edit switches between speakers on a studio set. The clip ends when the idea lands.

name: Everyday clip with a comment trap
aka: comment bait clip; the comments carry the joke
shape: An ordinary video of daily life that leaves one obvious, funny gap: something odd in the frame, a missing detail, a choice that makes no sense. Viewers rush to the comments to point it out. The top comment that fills the gap becomes the payoff, and the creator often plants it or pins it quickly.

name: Open question that starts an argument
aka: debate question; comment question; what's your answer
shape: The speaker asks one question to camera, a question with many valid answers that people hold strong opinions about. They give a few framing details, then give their own answer at the very end or keep it to themselves. The comments become the content.

name: Send this to someone
aka: share this with; send it to your partner; tag someone list
shape: The speaker opens by naming a specific person the viewer knows ("your partner", "your CFO") and tells them to send the video to that person. Then comes a short list built for that pair: questions to ask, tests to try, lines to use. The instruction to share is part of the content.

name: Golden ticket hunt
aka: hidden prize; treasure hunt giveaway; find the ticket
shape: The creator announces in the first seconds that a prize is hidden somewhere the audience must look: in the comments, inside a product order, or in a frame of the video. They show the prize and state the rule. The rest of the video teases where it might be and pushes people to search.

name: Tech office satire skit
aka: tech humour skit; startup satire; corporate tech skit
shape: A short scripted scene exaggerates a situation everyone in tech recognizes: the ex big tech lead who brings it up constantly, the meeting taken from bed, the investor who mocks a pitch deck. One or two people play the roles in a real office or home setup. The scene builds to one punchline and stops.

name: Workplace sitcom with recurring characters
aka: office sitcom; team skit series; company sitcom
shape: The real team plays itself in short episodes shot in the real office. Each episode has one situation from the job and one punchline, usually between two people in frame. The same characters return, so viewers start following them like a show.

name: The impossible client request (phone call)
aka: crazy client call; extreme request; can you do this call
shape: A client calls with an extreme request, and the call plays on speaker in the office. The team listens, reacts, and works out the solution live, on whiteboards, screens or phones. The video ends on the answer to the client, which shows how the service handles the impossible.

name: Guess the client from the mess
aka: what kind of customer left this; guess the customer
shape: Two team members look at what a customer left behind (a cabin, a desk, a cart, a workspace) and guess the type of customer from the clues. Quick rounds, one clue at a time, and a verdict at the end of each. The viewer plays along.

name: The boss wants more videos (reluctant employee tour)
aka: reluctant employee; deadpan shop tour; boss made me do this
shape: An employee films the workplace with deadpan reluctance and explains they are only doing it because "the boss wants more videos". They walk through the place and list the products in the flattest voice possible. The anti-ad tone is the ad.

name: Hey Boss: the comment question, asked on the shop floor
aka: Hey Boss; comment question on the floor; ask the boss
shape: An employee walks up to the boss in the middle of work, phone in hand, and reads a question from the comments out loud ("Hey boss, someone asks..."). The boss answers on the spot, often by showing the product or the machine. The comment appears on screen while it is read.

name: Crying-filter employee interview
aka: do you like working here trend; crying filter trend
shape: Someone off camera asks employees, one after another, "do you like working here?". Each answers with enthusiasm while a crying filter on their face says the opposite. The gap between the words and the filter is the joke, and the clip works as light, self-aware employer branding.

name: Workplace trivia gotcha
aka: did you know bet; colleague bet; product trivia skit
shape: One employee bets a colleague on a surprising fact about something in their own workplace. The colleague doubts it out loud. The proof is shown on the spot, in one shot, and the colleague reacts.

name: Mockumentary of an absurd expert
aka: mock documentary; absurd expert portrait; fake documentary
shape: A documentary-style portrait of a fictional expert who carries one absurd contradiction ("the only beekeeper allergic to bee stings"). The character speaks to an interviewer off camera, with workplace shots in between, all played seriously. The comedy comes from the straight face.

name: The last one doing it by hand (satire character)
aka: artisanal hand coder; the last of the old way; proud manual worker
shape: A character speaks to camera and proudly presents himself as one of the last people doing a job the old way. He describes his craft with the solemnity of an artisan. Every line, without saying it, mocks the old way that the product replaces.

name: Roleplay: wrong answer vs right answer
aka: bad answer good answer; play it twice; answer makeover
shape: A real-life scene (a job interview, a sales call, a negotiation) is played twice. First comes the answer most people give and its weak result. Then the same scene replays with the answer that works and its better result.

name: Namesake stunt (a regular person with a famous rival's name)
aka: namesake review; same name stunt; rival namesake
shape: The brand finds an ordinary person who shares the name of a famous figure linked to a rival, such as a competitor's CEO. That person introduces themselves by full name to camera, then uses or praises the brand's product like any happy customer. The name does the joke; the review stays sincere.

name: Movie scene remake with your product
aka: film scene parody; iconic scene remake; product movie parody
shape: The team reenacts a famous film scene line for line, in their own workplace. The product takes the place of the iconic object at the center of the scene. Viewers recognize the scene in seconds and wait for the product's moment.

name: Trend sound, then the product
aka: trend intro; trend hook then product; sound hook
shape: The first seconds ride a trending sound or a short sketch everyone recognizes. Then the video switches to the product or the workplace: how it is made, packed or used. The trend buys the attention, the product keeps it.

name: Absurd narration with the product as hero
aka: brainrot narration; epic narration; deadpan voice-over story
shape: A deadpan or absurd voice tells a made-up epic about an ordinary situation, over simple footage. The story escalates far beyond what the images show. The product or the team becomes the hero who saves the day, in the same overblown tone (the "brainrot" register).

name: POV skit: the product saves the moment
aka: POV rescue; POV product save
shape: "POV:" text on screen sets an everyday crisis. The scene is filmed in first person, so the viewer lives the problem. Then the product arrives and saves the moment, in one quick, visible action.

name: Mock museum: a mundane object presented as art
aka: office art critic; workplace museum; fake art installation
shape: The camera moves slowly around a mundane object of the workplace, framed like a piece in a gallery. A solemn voice, in the tone of an art critic, gives it a title, a year, an artist and a deep interpretation. The more ordinary the object, the funnier the reading.

name: Song about your product
aka: product jingle; brand song; parody song
shape: An original song or a parody tells the product's job or the customer's daily pain, over b-roll of the product in use. Verses describe the problem in a funny, specific way. The chorus is the product promise, short enough to stick.

name: Split-screen face-off (us vs them)
aka: us vs them; old way vs new way; face-off
shape: Two sides of a cliché face off on a split screen: two countries, two jobs, the old way and the new way. Each side answers the other line for line, often played by the same person. The exchange escalates until one side wins or both look absurd.

name: Drawn skit (illustrated situation)
aka: illustrated skit; drawing storytime; animated sketch
shape: A situation from daily life is acted out with drawings, sketched live or animated simply. One voice plays every role, changing tone for each character. No face appears: the drawings and the voice carry the scene.

name: Smart-glasses street prank (demo at the end)
aka: smart glasses prank; POV glasses challenge; street prank with a reveal
shape: Filmed through smart glasses, the creator challenges strangers to a game or a task and wins thanks to what the glasses show or whisper. The stranger's reaction carries the video. The last seconds reveal the device and show how it worked.

name: Street interview: one question about your market
aka: micro-trottoir; vox pop; one question street interview
shape: The interviewer asks the same single question about a market to strangers, or to people who work in that field, in the place where they gather. The answers are cut fast, one after another, a few seconds each. The video ends on the best or the most surprising answer.

name: Product on the street: guess the price
aka: how much does this cost; street price guess; guess the price
shape: The interviewer hands the product, or shows it on a phone, to someone on the street and asks how much it costs. The person guesses, and the real answer reveals a business model they did not expect. Their next question becomes the objection the video answers.

name: Street riddle
aka: street trick question; riddle on the street; brain teaser interview
shape: The interviewer reads the same trick question to several passers-by. They answer fast, often wrong, and the edit lets the viewer watch them think. The video ends when one person finds the right answer, or with the answer on screen.

name: Prove-it quiz: the self-proclaimed genius
aka: tell me this genius; prove you are smart; Stanford quiz
shape: A person boasts about being very smart, with a school or an IQ as proof. The interviewer answers with a real technical question from a field, word for word. The answer, right or wrong, is the payoff, and the correct reasoning closes the video.

name: Expert takes on a challenger
aka: expert versus challenger; prove it live; street debate challenge
shape: The expert accepts a live challenge from an opponent: a match, a debate or a test. Both sit or stand in the same frame, and the contest runs on camera. The outcome is unknown when filming starts, and the video ends on the result.

name: I tested a celebrity's routine
aka: I tried a famous person's routine; celebrity diet test; I lived like a famous CEO
shape: The creator picks the routine, diet, workout or method of a famous person and follows it for real, for a day, a week or longer. The video shows the attempt in short scenes, with the hard moments kept in. It ends with an honest verdict on what worked and what did not.

name: Product torture test: which one wins?
aka: torture test; which one is faster; head to head test
shape: The product and its alternatives go through the same test in the real world: speed, power, resistance. The video shows the setup, the measurement for each one and the moment one of them fails or wins. It ends on a clear winner.

name: Blind test
aka: taste test; guess which one; blind comparison
shape: Two things are compared without saying which is which. A person tries both, judges them out loud and picks one. The reveal shows which was which, and the person's reaction closes the video.

name: Real-life quest series
aka: quest series; I'm trying to find; follow my journey
shape: The creator sets a real goal with an uncertain outcome: find a stolen object, meet someone, reach a hard-to-reach person or place. Each episode follows one step of the search, with leads, setbacks and progress. Every episode ends with an open question, and viewers return for the ending.

name: Daily challenge until the goal (day X of Y)
aka: day X of Y; daily challenge; 365 days challenge
shape: The creator repeats the same act every day and posts it with a visible counter ("Day 214 of 365"). Each video is short and looks almost the same, with one small change: a little progress, a new obstacle, a different place. The counter and the stubbornness are the story.

name: Public spectacle stunt
aka: flash mob; public stunt; guerrilla stunt
shape: A spectacle happens in a public place: a flash mob, a machine in a stadium, an event announced out of nowhere. Several cameras film the action and the crowd's reaction. The scale of the moment is the message, and the brand appears at the end or in the caption.

name: App demo in the real place
aka: in-context demo; field demo; use it where it happens
shape: The app is used where the problem happens: in the supermarket, on the job site, at the front desk. A real case is solved from start to finish. The edit cuts between the place and the phone or laptop screen at each step.

name: Feature parade: have you ever struggled with X?
aka: have you ever struggled; problem solution montage; feature montage
shape: A fast series of small everyday problems, each introduced with "Have you ever struggled with...?". After each question, one feature solves the problem on screen in a few seconds. The rhythm is question, solution, next question, until the last and most surprising feature.

name: Bad news hook: the problem you did not know you had
aka: I got bad news; hidden flaw reveal; problem agitation demo
shape: The video opens with "I got bad news" and reveals a hidden flaw in something the viewer uses every day. It proves the flaw visually, with a close-up, a slow-motion or an animated graph. Then it introduces the product that fixes the flaw and shows the difference.

name: Why this does not exist (until now)
aka: why doesn't this exist; the obvious product nobody made; impossible product explained
shape: The video asks why an obvious product has never been made. It explains the technical reason, often with a simple animation or a test on a bench. Then it shows how the team solved the problem, with the product working.

name: Build it yourself (for a fraction of the price)
aka: so I built my own; DIY versus expensive; I built it in a weekend
shape: The maker shows an expensive product and its price, then says they built their own for much less. The video follows the build in fast steps. It ends with the home-made version working and one reason it suits them better.

name: Satisfying making-of
aka: oddly satisfying; how it's made; ASMR making-of
shape: A machine or a pair of hands makes the product from start to finish, filmed in close-up. The real sound of the process carries the video, with no talking. It ends on the finished product, held up or in use.

name: Custom order for a famous client
aka: we received a letter from; famous client order; special commission
shape: The maker opens with "We received a letter from" and names a famous client. They tell the request, then design and make the custom piece on camera. The video ends on the finished result.

name: Unboxing as a ritual
aka: satisfying unboxing; ASMR unboxing; slow unboxing
shape: The product is opened slowly, layer by layer, in close-up. Every seal, flap and insert is shown with its real sound. The video ends with the first use of the product.

name: Tier list of your own products
aka: ranking our own products; founders rank their products; which one we prefer
shape: The founders rank their own products, features or plans from best to worst, on a tier board in frame. Each item gets a place and a reason, and the founders argue when they disagree. The honest low rankings are the point: they show the team knows its weak spots.

name: Tier list of the options in your market
aka: market tier list; ranking the tools; best to worst
shape: The creator ranks the tools, methods or options of a market from best to worst, one item at a time, with one reason each. The tier board stays on screen, behind the speaker or as a carousel. The founder's own product stays out of the ranking, so the video reads as expertise.

name: Staged in-store discovery
aka: shelf discovery skit; wait they have it here; found it in store
shape: Two people walk past a place where the product is available and stop as if they just spotted it. One of them reacts with surprise ("wait, they have it here?"), picks it up and the pair tell each other why they love it. The video ends on the product in hand and where to find it.

name: Creator skit with the product woven in
aka: integrated sponsorship skit; product placement skit; branded comedy skit
shape: A creator runs their usual comedy skit, with the same characters and tone their audience knows. The product appears as a natural part of the story: it solves the problem in the plot, causes the twist or becomes the running gag. The partnership is disclosed, and the skit ends on a joke that brings the product back once more.

name: Too good to be true? Expert product test
aka: claim test; does it really work?; expert review
shape: An expert opens with the product's claim that sounds too good to believe, for example a price far below the only similar device. They test it on real use, in their own setting. They give a verdict that names what holds up and where the limits are.

name: Customer testimonial in UGC style
aka: UGC testimonial; selfie testimonial; customer story
shape: A real customer films themselves with a phone, at home or at work. In their own words they tell how things were before, the moment it changed and what is different now. The framing stays simple, with maybe one shot of the product in use.

name: Dear brand, we need to talk
aka: open letter to a brand; can we talk about what you built?; brand callout
shape: The creator speaks straight to a brand, tagging it in the opening line, about a product so extreme it deserves a talk. They walk through what makes it excessive, with b-roll of the product. They mix real admiration with jokes about the kind of person who buys it.

name: Watch this before you buy
aka: buyer's guide; watch this before buying; mistakes to avoid when buying
shape: The video lists the mistakes buyers make when they choose a product in one category. Each mistake is shown with a real install, a test or a side by side. The video ends on a short checklist the viewer can screenshot before buying.

name: Cinematic product film
aka: product film; launch film; brand film
shape: A short film made with film-grade shots, lighting and music, with very few words. The product is revealed slowly, detail by detail, as if it were an event. It ends on the product in full and one line of text or voice.

name: Event teaser trailer
aka: event trailer; aftermovie teaser; save the date trailer
shape: A trailer cut like a movie preview, with epic music and fast shots from a past edition of the event. The energy builds with each cut: crowd, speakers, details, laughter. It ends on the date, the place and the call to book.

name: The quiet demo: the tool appears, nobody names it
aka: unnamed demo; comment-bait demo; silent product placement
shape: You post a useful video on a topic your buyers care about, and you use your product on screen to get the result. You never name it or point at it. Viewers who notice ask "what tool is that?" in the comments, and the answer goes there.

name: Unusual job, with the numbers
aka: behind the operation; the job nobody sees; operations in numbers
shape: The video shows an operation nobody usually sees, filmed where it happens. A few striking numbers carry it: weight, people, hours, distance. A pun or a light line closes it.

name: Startup war-room tour
aka: war room; team tour; it's 2 a.m. and we're locked in
shape: At a key moment (2 a.m. before a launch, the last night of a sprint), the camera walks through the team at work. Each person gets one line: who they are and what they are doing right now. The tour ends on the person running the show or on the thing about to ship.

name: Dream client turned nightmare
aka: worst client story; biggest disappointment; client horror story
shape: The founder tells, to camera, how a dream client arrived, why it felt like a big break, what went wrong step by step, and what they learned. The client is never named or identifiable. It is filmed where the work happens, with a few cutaways to the work itself.

name: Everyone does this, don't
aka: common mistake on site; stop doing this; the better way
shape: The expert points at a common setup, the way almost everyone does it. They say it is exactly what to avoid and explain why in one sentence. Then they show the better way on site, with the result visible.

name: 24-hour makeover of someone's brand
aka: brand makeover; 24-hour rebrand; website makeover challenge
shape: The team picks a small business and redoes its brand, page or shop under a time limit. The video shows the before, the process at speed and the reveal to the owner. The owner's reaction closes it.

name: Business rescue episode
aka: rescue show; business makeover show; expert to the rescue
shape: An expert arrives in a struggling business, in the style of TV rescue shows. They observe, diagnose the problems with the owner, change a few things and leave. Later they come back to measure what changed, and the owner says how it went.

name: Two founders, two paths
aka: bootstrap vs raise; founder versus; same question two answers
shape: Two founders who made opposite choices (bootstrap or raise, solo or cofounders) sit side by side. A host asks them the same questions and they answer in turn. Nobody declares a winner: the viewer judges and says so in the comments.

name: I sat down with a big name
aka: I sat down with; interview clip; big guest short
shape: The video opens with "I sat down with [famous person]" and drops the most surprising claim of the interview right away. Then it gives the context: who the guest is and why their opinion matters. It ends on one follow-up question and the guest's answer.

name: Text on a still (meme)
aka: text meme; relatable meme; one-liner on an image
shape: One image or a very short clip fills the screen, with one line of text on top. The text says something your audience recognizes from their own life. There is no voice: the image, the line and often a trending sound do the work.

name: Photo carousel story
aka: photo mode; slideshow; carousel
shape: A swipeable set of photos, with one line of text per slide. The slides tell a story, a timeline or a list, one step at a time. The last slide is the payoff: the result, the answer or the lesson.

name: Off-camera interview: the story of one order (big-claim textbox)
aka: behind-the-deal interview; broker story interview; the order that changed everything
shape: The founder sits or stands where the business happens and answers an interviewer who stays off camera. They tell the story of one order: who called, what they asked for, what went wrong or what it cost. A big claim sits on screen as a textbox the whole time, and the best stories continue as part 2 and part 3.

name: Newsjack, then make it with your product
aka: news reaction with a product twist; make the news; same-day newsjack
shape: A hot news item or a meme of the day plays first, with a short reaction from the founder or a teammate. Then the team makes something about that news with the product: an object, an image, a page, a result. The video ends on the thing they made, held up or shown on screen.

name: Car interview cut into one video per feature
aka: car yapping interview; passenger seat interview; the car is a studio
shape: A teammate in the passenger seat asks the founder questions during a drive, with the phone on a mount. Each answer about one feature becomes its own video, with a claim textbox on top. The answer cuts to a screen recording of that feature in action, then back to the car.

name: The new hire learns one task (numbered episodes)
aka: the new guy; onboarding sketch series; new hire episode 1
shape: A new team member tries one task of the job and gets it wrong in a funny way. The boss or a senior colleague corrects them and shows the right way. Each episode has a number and the same textbox pattern ("How to do X: the new hire, ep 3").

name: Staged job interview in parts
aka: fake job interview; hard interview with this candidate; interview sketch part 1
shape: A staged job interview plays out across a table: the founder or boss on one side, an unusual candidate on the other. One textbox stays on top for the whole video ("Tough interview with this candidate"), and a short "part 2" label flashes in the centre for a few seconds. Each part ends at a moment that makes viewers want the next one.

name: React to a viral clip, then redo it in your app
aka: reaction plus app replay; viral clip rebuilt in the product; reaction to demo
shape: A viral clip from someone else plays with a short, funny reaction: a trip, a workout, a recipe, a room makeover. Then the screen switches to the app, where the same thing is rebuilt: the route traced, the plan generated, the budget computed. The video ends on the result in the app, next to a frame of the original clip.

name: Bad buzz answered one viral video at a time
aka: crisis response reactions; answer the backlash; founder faces the bad buzz
shape: When videos attacking the company or its product go viral, the founder answers them one by one, as reactions. Each video plays a few seconds of one attack, then the founder says what is fair in it and answers one argument with a fact. The series starts with the most watched attack and moves down the list.

name: Snap transition: empty to finished, on a loop
aka: finger snap transition; empty to set up; looping before and after
shape: Someone snaps their fingers or taps a surface, and the scene jumps to empty. Short shots then show it being set up piece by piece, from a fixed camera. In the last shot the person walks back into the same position as the first frame, so the video loops without a visible cut.

name: Deadpan sigma coach parody
aka: sigma male parody; alpha coach parody; deadpan motivational pitch
shape: A team member speaks to camera like a self-proclaimed "sigma" coach: slow voice, total seriousness, grand claims about discipline and status. The subject is an ordinary product, treated as the mark of a superior person ("You are a sigma. Your spreadsheet does not show it."). Objections are mocked, the call to action lands, then a long pause and a punchline.

name: Subtle foreshadowing: tease the disaster, then the steps
aka: subtle foreshadowing trend; tease the fail; flash-forward disaster
shape: A clean step-by-step process plays (a recipe, a setup, a build), but short flashes of a disaster to come are cut between the steps: a hand about to ruin it, a scream, a spill. The steps continue calmly while the flashes grow longer. The disaster finally happens in full at the end, and the reaction closes the video.

name: Character core compilation
aka: POV founder core; X core edit; personality montage
shape: A fast montage of short moments that show one person's personality: they get annoyed, laugh, help someone, look exhausted, celebrate. The clips come from behind-the-scenes footage, cut to music in the style of celebrity fan edits. A textbox names the person as a "core" ("POV: [name] core").

name: I let my Gen Z intern edit this video
aka: intern edit trend; Gen Z edit; chaotic intern edit
shape: An ordinary company video, re-edited in a deliberately chaotic style: sudden zooms, meme sounds, captions with slang, random effects. A textbox at the start says the intern was given the edit. The contrast between a serious brand and the wild edit carries the joke.

name: I lied on my CV to run these socials
aka: fake resume edit; social media manager confession; help me keep my job
shape: A long textbox sits over existing footage of the company: the person behind the account confesses they lied on their CV to get the job and now must run the social media of an unlikely boss or business. The footage shows that boss or business doing its thing. The text ends with a plea: "help me keep my job".

name: Three-intensity hook stack ad
aka: hook stacking ad; safe middle max hooks; three hooks three settings
shape: One ad body is shot once, and three hooks are shot separately at three intensities, each in its own setting. The safe hook is filmed at the desk and stacks authority, the middle hook in a meeting room, the bold hook outdoors and sounds the most personal. Each hook makes the right viewer recognize themselves, then the same body runs: problem, solution, origin story, metaphor, a case with numbers, proof, and a call to book a short eligibility call.

name: Video game killcam on real footage
aka: killcam edit; kill counter overlay; real life as a shooter game
shape: First-person footage of a real activity (a race, a sales day, a sprint at work) is edited like a video game. Every small win triggers a game announcer sound and adds one to a kill counter on screen. A few staged setbacks add drama, and the counter ends on a final score.

name: Persona callout ad with a qualifying CTA
aka: B2B leadgen ad; call out the buyer; come prepared CTA
shape: The ad opens by naming one buyer role and one problem they own ("Ops leaders: your onboarding is costing you hires. Let me show you."). The founder introduces themselves, then the video shows the product or the work, the options, and four before-and-after results. The call to action filters leads: it tells viewers what to have ready before they book.
